```{python setup}
def hatch_wall(ax, x, y0, y1, side=1, n=7, size=0.28, color=INK, lw=1.3):
    """A fixed-support wall: a solid line with hatching on one side."""
    ax.plot([x, x], [y0, y1], color=color, lw=lw * 1.4, zorder=6)
    for yv in np.linspace(y0, y1, n):
        ax.plot([x, x + side * size], [yv, yv - size], color=color, lw=lw,
                zorder=6)
```

How do we synthesize both of these concepts, as well as e.g. flow of fluid, transport of a
contaminant, current through a medium, etc.

Generalize & express as a **boundary value** (time independent) **or initial value** (time
dependent) **problem**.

Consider the deformation of a one-dimensional beam.

# 1D Axial Deformation Derivation

```{python fig_bar}
#| echo: false
#| output: false

L_BAR = 8.0

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.6, 2.6))
m = Model()
m.add_node(Node("A", 0.0, 0.0, hide_dot=True, hide_id=True))
m.add_node(Node("B", L_BAR, 0.0, hide_dot=True, hide_id=True))
m.add_element(Element("E1", "A", "B", kind="beam", color=INK, linewidth=2.6))
# the axial end force, and the distributed axial load q(x)
m.add_load(PointLoad("A", fx=1.0, scale=0.62, points_to_loc=True, label="$F$",
                     color=INK, text_size=13, label_xalign="right",
                     label_yalign="bottom"))
# stop the arrows short of the wall so the last one does not run into it
m.add_load(DistLoad("E1", wx_start=1.0, wx_end=1.0, end_offset=0.90,
                    points_to_loc=False, n_arrows=8, scale=0.30,
                    label="$q(x)$", color=INK, text_size=13))
m.add_dimension(Dimension("A", "B", kind="x", label="$L$", offset=-0.55,
                          color=DIMCLR, text_size=13))
m.plot(ax=ax, show_node_labels=False, show_element_labels=False,
       show_axes=False, node_size=0)

hatch_wall(ax, L_BAR, -0.42, 0.42, side=1, n=6, size=0.34)
ax.annotate("", xy=(1.35, -0.62), xytext=(0.15, -0.62),
            arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-|>", color=INK, lw=1.2,
                            mutation_scale=11))
ax.plot([0.15, 0.15], [-0.78, -0.46], color=INK, lw=1.2)
ax.text(1.45, -0.62, "$x, u$", color=INK, ha="left", va="center", fontsize=13)

tidy(ax)
ax.set_xlim(-1.8, L_BAR + 1.6)

```

::: {.step}
![](`{python} fig_bar_path`){#fig-c2-bar width=76%}
:::

Assume a structural member loaded axially, both by a force at its end, $F$, and a
distributed axial loading, $q$.

Assume the bar is of length $L$, $x$ is the position along the bar from the LHS, & $u$ is
displacement (as a function of $x$) in the rightward direction. Assume a constant
cross-section, $A$.

Let $Q_c = \left(\int q\,dx + C\right)$ be the pre-derivative of $q$.

Choose an "element" of the bar


::: {.step}
![](`{python} fig_element_path`){#fig-c2-element width=56%}
:::

Sum the forces for this element:

::: {.derivation}
$$
\begin{aligned}
\sum F_x = 0 \;\Rightarrow\;& -A\sigma(x) + A\sigma(x+\Delta x)
   + \int_x^{x+\Delta x} q(y)\,dy = 0 \\[4pt]
\Rightarrow\;& A\big[\sigma(x+\Delta x) - \sigma(x)\big]
   + Q_c(x+\Delta x) - Q_c(x) = 0 \\[4pt]
\Rightarrow\;& \frac{1}{\Delta x}\Big[A\big[\sigma(x+\Delta x)-\sigma(x)\big]
   + Q_c(x+\Delta x) - Q_c(x)\Big] = 0
   \qquad \text{b.c. } \Delta x \neq 0 \\[4pt]
\Rightarrow\;& A\left[\frac{\sigma(x+\Delta x)-\sigma(x)}{\Delta x}\right]
   + \frac{Q_c(x+\Delta x)-Q_c(x)}{\Delta x} = 0
\end{aligned}
$$
:::

::: {.step}
$\displaystyle \lim_{\Delta x \to 0}$
:::

::: {.derivation}
$$
\begin{aligned}
\Rightarrow\;& A\frac{d\sigma}{dx} + \frac{dQ_c}{dx} = 0 \\[4pt]
\Rightarrow\;& A\frac{d\sigma}{dx} + q(x) = 0
   && \text{(Fundamental Theorem of Calculus)} \\[4pt]
\Rightarrow\;& AE\frac{d\varepsilon}{dx} + q(x) = 0
   && \text{(Hooke's Law: } \sigma = E\varepsilon) \\[4pt]
\Rightarrow\;& \boxed{AE\frac{d^2u}{dx^2} + q(x) = 0}
   && \left(\varepsilon = \frac{du}{dx}
      = \lim_{\Delta x \to 0}\frac{\Delta \ell}{\Delta x}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$
:::

Now,

::: {.derivation}
$$
\begin{aligned}
u(L) &= 0 && \text{(Fixed end)} \\[6pt]
F &= \left.\frac{A\sigma}{A}\right|_{x=0}
   = \left.\frac{AE\varepsilon}{A}\right|_{x=0}
   = \left.AE\frac{du}{dx}\right|_{x=0}
   && \text{(Force on the end)} \\[4pt]
&\Rightarrow\; \left.\frac{du}{dx}\right|_{x=0} = \frac{F}{EA}
\end{aligned}
$$
:::

## In Summary

::: {.derivation}
$$
\frac{d^2u}{dx^2} + \frac{q(x)}{EA} = 0
\qquad
u(L) = 0
\qquad
\left.\frac{du}{dx}\right|_{x=0} = \frac{F}{EA}
$$
:::

Define

::: {.derivation}
$$
f(x) = \frac{q(x)}{EA}
\qquad\qquad
h = \frac{-F}{EA}
$$
:::

Then our problem matches the Hughes FEM book:

::: {.derivation}
$$
\frac{d^2u}{dx^2} + f(x) = 0
\qquad
u(L) = 0
\qquad
-\frac{du}{dx} = h
\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad
\left(\;
\begin{aligned}
u_{,xx} + f &= 0 \\
u(L) &= 0 \\
-u_{,x} &= h
\end{aligned}
\;\right)
$$
:::

# The Poisson equation

Many problems, including heat transfer, flow of water in an aquifer, electromagnetic
potential, & 1D rod deformation can be written using Laplace's / Poisson's Equation.

::: {.derivation}
$$
(\mathrm{S})\quad
\begin{cases}
\dfrac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x^2} + f = 0
  & \leftarrow \text{Poisson equation} \\[10pt]
u(L) = g
  & \leftarrow \text{known, or \textbf{Dirichlet} boundary condition} \\[10pt]
-\dfrac{du}{dx} = h
  & \leftarrow \text{flux-based, or \textbf{Neumann} boundary condition}
\end{cases}
$$
:::

Here, in reality, $u$ is our unknown quantity; $f$, $g$ & $h$ are inputs.

In language of math, $u$ is a function — write

::: {.step}
$u : [0, L] \longrightarrow \mathbb{R}$
:::

::: {.step .notes}
- the domain is the kinds of input locations
- the range is the expected kinds of output ($\mathbb{R}$ is real #s)
:::

$(\mathrm{S})$ is a boundary value problem, with the two boundary conditions only examples
of types of boundary conditions.

## In higher dimensions

In higher dimensions, the Poisson Equation is as follows, with the Laplace equation being
the case when $f = 0$.

Given $f : \Omega \to \mathbb{R}$, $h : \Gamma_h \to \mathbb{R}$,
$g : \Gamma_g \to \mathbb{R}$, find $u \in H^1(\Omega)$ such that

::: {.derivation}
$$
\begin{aligned}
-\Delta u &= f && \text{in } \Omega && \leftarrow \text{Poisson equation} \\
u &= g && \text{on } \Gamma_g && \leftarrow \text{known values} \\
\nabla u \cdot \underline{n} &= h && \text{on } \Gamma_h && \leftarrow \text{known flux}
\end{aligned}
$$
:::

Or, more generally, for anisotropic behavior, assuming $\underline{\underline{K}}$ is also
known, find $u$ such that

::: {.derivation}
$$
\begin{aligned}
-\nabla \cdot \left(\underline{\underline{K}}\nabla u\right) &= f && \text{in } \Omega \\
u &= g && \text{on } \Gamma_g \\
\nabla\left(\underline{\underline{K}}u\right)\cdot \underline{n} &= h && \text{on } \Gamma_h
\end{aligned}
$$
:::

```{python fig_domain}
#| echo: false
#| output: false

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10.6, 3.6),
                         gridspec_kw={"width_ratios": [1.0, 1.05]})

# ---- a general domain ------------------------------------------------------
ax = axes[0]
t = np.linspace(0, 2 * math.pi, 400)
r = 2.3 + 0.30 * np.sin(3 * t) + 0.18 * np.cos(5 * t)
X, Y = r * np.cos(t), r * np.sin(t)
ax.fill(X, Y, color=DOMCLR, alpha=0.55, zorder=1)
top = (t > 0.35 * math.pi) & (t < 0.95 * math.pi)
ax.plot(X, Y, color=BDRYCLR, lw=2.0, zorder=3)
ax.plot(X[top], Y[top], color=FLUXCLR, lw=3.2, zorder=4)
ax.text(0.0, 0.0, r"$\Omega$", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=17, color=INK)
ax.text(X[top][len(X[top]) // 2] - 0.1, Y[top][len(Y[top]) // 2] + 0.45,
        r"$\Gamma_h$", ha="center", va="bottom", fontsize=14, color=FLUXCLR)
ax.text(0.9, -2.75, r"$\Gamma_g$", ha="center", va="top", fontsize=14,
        color=BDRYCLR)
tidy(ax)
ax.set_xlim(-3.4, 3.4); ax.set_ylim(-3.6, 3.4)

# ---- an I-beam cross-section ------------------------------------------------
ax = axes[1]
bw, bt, wh, ww = 3.4, 0.34, 2.1, 0.42
parts = [(-bw / 2, wh / 2, bw, bt), (-bw / 2, -wh / 2 - bt, bw, bt),
         (-ww / 2, -wh / 2, ww, wh)]
for (px, py, pw, ph) in parts:
    ax.add_patch(plt.Rectangle((px, py), pw, ph, facecolor=DOMCLR,
                               edgecolor=BDRYCLR, lw=1.8, alpha=0.75, zorder=2))
ax.plot([-bw / 2, bw / 2], [wh / 2 + bt, wh / 2 + bt], color=FLUXCLR, lw=3.4,
        zorder=5)
ax.text(0.0, wh / 2 + bt + 0.22, r"$\Gamma_h$", ha="center", va="bottom",
        fontsize=14, color=FLUXCLR)
ax.text(0.0, -wh / 2 - bt - 0.28, r"$\Gamma_g$", ha="center", va="top",
        fontsize=14, color=BDRYCLR)
ax.text(ww / 2 + 0.35, 0.0, r"$\Omega$", ha="left", va="center", fontsize=16,
        color=INK)
tidy(ax)
ax.set_xlim(-2.9, 2.9); ax.set_ylim(-2.6, 2.4)

fig.subplots_adjust(wspace=0.05)
fig_domain_path = save(fig, "C2_Fig5_Domain.png")
```

![](`{python} fig_domain_path`){#fig-c2-domain width=94%}

::: {.notes}
- $\Omega$ is the geometry of interest (called the "domain")
- $\partial\Omega \equiv \Gamma$ is the boundary of the domain
- $\Gamma_g$ is the part of the boundary where we know $u = g$
- $\Gamma_h$ is the part of the boundary where we know the flux
:::

The entire boundary is such that

::: {.derivation}
$$
\Gamma = \Gamma_g \cup \Gamma_h
\qquad\qquad
\Gamma_g \cap \Gamma_h = \emptyset
$$
:::

::: {.step .notes}
- $\cup$ &nbsp; union
- $\cap$ &nbsp; intersect
- $\emptyset$ &nbsp; empty set (nothing)
:::
